1015.title: Artificial Intelligence, Consent, and the Limits of Production
1015.summary: Type foundries' stances on artificial intelligence emerged this month through three distinct approaches. Mass Driver announced that it does not use artificial intelligence at any stage of its design and production process. The manifesto-like text frames type design as a field of production tied to human labor,…
1015.content:
Type foundries' stances on artificial intelligence emerged this month through three distinct approaches. Mass Driver [announced](https://mass-driver.com/article/from-human-hands) that it does not use artificial intelligence at any stage of its design and production process. The manifesto-like text frames type design as a field of production tied to human labor, experience, and thought processes. TypeType, while acknowledging that AI accelerates design production, [argues](https://typetype.medium.com/why-unique-fonts-matter-even-in-the-age-of-ai-generated-design-2cc7c2bdbb36) that original, custom-designed typefaces play a critical role in helping brands maintain their distinctive identities in the face of widespread AI-generated design. While one side rejects AI entirely, the other accepts it as a tool but places the human designer and their originality at the heart of design. The third approach is seen in [ShieldFont](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/fonts-typography/type-designers-have-created-a-free-font-that-poisons-ai), jointly developed by Seneda & Abrucio and Playtype. Appearing ordinary to the human eye yet presenting different words to AI web scrapers, this open-source typeface operates using OpenType glyph substitution. In controlled tests, 55.8 percent of the protected passages did not convey the same factual claim as the original text. The developers define ShieldFont not as "anti-AI," but as a de facto opt-out option guided by the principle "Publishing is not consent!" Rather than rejecting or embracing AI, consent is turned into a technical defense mechanism.

[NeuralType](https://elih.net/blog/neuraltype/), developed by Eli Heuer, moves in the exact opposite direction of these approaches. In this experimental format with an NTF extension, the font file itself is a neural network, and each letterform is generated based on context. The format aims to provide an alternative to OpenType's static glyph table-based approach, especially for cursive and context-sensitive writing systems such as Nastaliq. Developed as a demo, the typeface was built as a 1.36-million-parameter multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained on the forms of the open-font-licensed Gulzar typeface.

In contrast to this scenario where type is automatically generated from context, Dan Hollick [likens](https://www.makingsoftware.com/chapters/how-to-make-a-font) typeface production to an iterative process consisting of research, conceptual decisions, character set construction, metric adjustments, testing, and iteration. A successful typeface is determined not so much by individually aesthetic glyphs, but by how characters work consistently and legibly within text. This necessitates the constant testing of design decisions. While automation can increase speed, the evaluation process continues to require human judgment.

This limitation of automation is exemplified by the [web tool](https://blode.co/static-to-variable) developed by Matthew Blode. Blode's tool generates variable fonts by interpolating between uploaded static weights. When the output is inspected in type design software, the curves turn out to consist of straight line segments rather than true curves. Although this is not noticeable to the eye, technical quality is inevitably compromised.

Aiming to catch such issues earlier during the proofing stage, [Hellbox](https://hellbox.com/) is introduced as a macOS-exclusive app that monitors Glyphs files and generates updated PDF proof sheets with every save. Offered with a one-time $100 license, the tool also enables tasks such as generating proofs and inspecting fonts via natural language through AI assistants, thanks to its MCP support. It thereby aims to catch details that might otherwise be overlooked in font production earlier and make the quality control process more continuous. From another perspective, Hellbox establishes a new layer of control supporting human oversight in an environment where artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into the production process.

---

1016.title: The Technical and Political Layers of History
1016.summary: The principles of typography laid down by Jan Tschichold nearly a century ago have been brought back to the table. Published by Sorry Press, Matter Of's book "New New Typography" questions whether these principles still define contemporary design. Bringing historical examples together with contemporary typographic…
1016.content:
The principles of typography laid down by Jan Tschichold nearly a century ago have been brought back to the table. Published by Sorry Press, Matter Of's book "[New New Typography](https://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/matter-of-new-new-typography-graphic-design-publication-project-150726)" questions whether these principles still define contemporary design. Bringing historical examples together with contemporary typographic experiments, the work proposes an experimental and pluralistic anti-guide that treats typography not as a set of rigid rules, but within a web of political, cultural, and technological relations. Not a rulebook, but a way of questioning the rules…

To understand how and under what technical conditions these typographic rules emerged, however, one must look further back to the material production processes of type. R. Stanley Nelson's book "[The Typefounder's Hand Mould](https://www.oakknoll.com/pages/books/143247/r-stanley-nelson/typefounders-hand-mould-the)" examines in detail the history, fabrication, and use of the hand mould that made metal type casting possible in the history of Western printing. The result of more than fifty years of research, the book is presented as the first comprehensive monograph in English to provide a practical explanation of mould-making and typecasting processes alongside historical examples.

[Vicki Tinnel's article](https://typography.guru/journal/the-evolution-of-japanese-typography-from-the-edo-period-to-today-r83/) traces the history of multi-script writing systems in Japanese typography. Spanning from the Edo period to the present day, this history centers on the Tsukiji Type Foundry established during Meiji-era Westernization and Motogi Shozo. The co-existence of Chinese-derived characters, Japan's two native syllabaries, and Latin letters, along with debates over vertical and horizontal text direction, are examined through examples such as the multilingual design crisis at the 1998 Nagano Olympics.

Kathleen Meaney moves beyond the crisis of multilingual design to reveal the far harsher political history behind it. In her [article](https://www.typotheque.com/articles/from-a-trail-of-type-to-the-trail-of-tears), Meaney explores the journey from the Cherokee syllabary developed by Sequoyah in the 1820s, through its adaptation into typography, to the publication of the *Cherokee Phoenix* newspaper. She examines this process through the typographic forms of the era, situated at the intersection of the Cherokee Nation's efforts to preserve its cultural and political autonomy and the pressures of missionary work, Christianization, and assimilation policies. While the story is interrupted in 1834 when the printing press was seized by the Georgia militia, it continues with the re-establishment of Cherokee printing operations in the West following the 1838 Trail of Tears.

A record taking typography history beyond the printed page comes from David Loeb Weiss's 1978 documentary "[Farewell: Etaoin Shrdlu](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1MGjFKs9bnU)". Presenting the preparation of The New York Times' last issue printed with hot metal typesetting on July 2, 1978, the documentary chronicles the production environment of the era—from Ludlow and Linotype machines to proofing and page make-up. The replacement of Linotype by phototypesetting and electronic systems is recorded as a witness to the end of the mechanical typesetting era.

---

1017.title: From Street to Archive: Typographic Sources of Identity
1017.summary: The Noble Signs shop, which produces handcrafted signs for local businesses in New York, is the subject of an eponymous documentary. Following the workshop as it seeks to preserve endangered signs under the roof of a museum, the documentary treats sign making as an integral part of the city's visual language. In…
1017.content:
The Noble Signs shop, which produces handcrafted signs for local businesses in New York, is the subject of an eponymous [documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4cAt2CAptkw&t=134s). Following the workshop as it seeks to preserve endangered signs under the roof of a museum, the documentary treats sign making as an integral part of the city's visual language.

In Lagos, this role was taken a step further, directly into public sculpture. Lagos-based artist Dennis Osadebe transformed the hand-painted lettering adorning minibuses into monumental steel sculptures in the [This Is Lagos](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/this-is-lagos-turns-the-citys-hand-painted-typography-into-monumental-public-art/) project. Having developed a typeface named *Godspeed* from this street typography through months of field research, the first of Osadebe's five sculptures have been installed in the cities of Ikeja, Owode, and Berger.

This street-level material became the direct source of a corporate identity in Berlin. Stan Hema's branding for the Berlin Museum [establishes](https://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/stan-hema-berlin-museum-graphic-design-project-060826) a dynamic logo system fed by the city's own typographic fabric rather than a singular, static logo. The system draws from diverse urban sources ranging from U-Bahn station signage and Café Moskau's Moskau Grotesk on Karl-Marx-Allee to Futura Black Stencil found on post-war Charlottenburg signs and Berlin's Späti culture. Rather than a single uniform typographic voice, the city's various historical and cultural strata converge within the same visual repertoire.

The source of corporate identity can sometimes narrow down to a single historic letter. As part of its new visual identity developed with Societas, Werder Bremen created a custom club typeface called [Bruckmeyer Neue](https://www.werder.de/en/news/other-news/2026-2027/visual-identity-30072026), inspired by Günther Bruckmeyer's 1924 letter W. Developed around the values the club defines through the bold, human, down-to-earth concept of "plietsch", the new visual identity will be phased in over two to three years starting with the 2026–2027 season.

The French Football Federation's visual identity project, on the other hand, relies not on a single letter but on a pair of type families serving two distinct functions. Solstices Studio and Blaze Type designed the custom type families [France and Héritage](https://blazetype.eu/case-studies/fff-france-heritage/) for the national teams. In the eight-member system, *France* handles contemporary and functional communications, while *Héritage* carries applications tied to history, achievements, and memory.

The same interplay of memory and contemporaneity finds a formal solution in Jamie Clarke's [Reel](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/how-all-caps-lost-its-voice/) typeface. Combining the visual impact of capitals with the more human and conversational tone of lowercase letters, Clarke designed the lowercase characters to occupy the same visual area and density as uppercase letters. In response to the eroded power of all-caps usage, he proposes a headline voice that is more open and inviting of discussion.

The research behind tone sometimes reaches straight into the archives. In its identity for eyewear brand [Bonnie Clyde](https://mouthwash.studio/project/bonnie-clyde/), Mouthwash Studio conducted extensive research drawing from the Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare texts, and typography archives to design a custom logo (wordmark). Drawing on resources from the Herb Lubalin Study Center and the New York Public Library, the work adapts historical letterforms into a contemporary brand language. The project demonstrates how typographic research emerges not merely as a reference, but as a methodology directly shaping design decisions.

---

1018.title: Small Points
1018.summary: 🔍 FontBase expanded typeface discovery with two data tools. While Fontalog makes over 3.5 million typefaces searchable by visual characteristics such as contrast, x-height, proportion, and weight, Font Rankings ranks the most widely used typefaces daily and monthly based on usage data. 🧩 Developed by Chingru,…
1018.content:
🔍 FontBase expanded typeface discovery with two data tools. While [Fontalog](https://fontalog.xyz/) makes over 3.5 million typefaces searchable by visual characteristics such as contrast, x-height, proportion, and weight, [Font Rankings](https://fontba.se/tools/rankings) ranks the most widely used typefaces daily and monthly based on usage data.

🧩 Developed by Chingru, [FontColle](https://font.chingru.com/) provides dedicated filters for Google Fonts by OpenType features, variable font axes, writing systems, and color vs. monochrome distinctions; [discussions on TypeDrawers](https://typedrawers.com/discussion/5655/fontcolle-an-enhanced-google-fonts-filter) reveal that Unicode character filtering clashes with gaps in Google's subset definitions.

🎓 The [Type and Media](https://2026.typemedia.org/) master's program at the Royal Academy of Art, The Hague has published its 2025–2026 graduation projects.

♿ On August 13, Type.today [published](https://type.today/en/journal/hector-mangas) an interview with cognitive psychologist and Accessibility Tools founder Héctor Mangas. Mangas reports that in their survey of over a hundred designers, the biggest barrier to accessibility was aesthetic concern, followed by time and cost, and that most typefaces advertised as dyslexia-friendly have no backing in the scientific literature.

🗣️ Yaprak Buse Çağlar will deliver a talk titled "Designing against forgetting" at [Rencontres de Lure](https://delure.org/les-rencontres/toutes-les-rencontres/rencontres-2026), to be held in France on August 22–27. Through the Aksan typeface, developed with inspiration from Turkey's Alphabet Reform, and research conducted at ANRT, she transforms historical forms into contemporary typographic systems.

1621.title: Responsibility, Ownership, and the Measure of Labor
1621.summary: The inclusion of Alexandra Korolkova in the program of ATypI’s conference held in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, between October 28–31, 2026, led to the withdrawal of two Ukrainian speakers. Oleksandra Korchevska-Tsekhosh and Oleksii Chekal, alongside the Ukrainian design community, sent an open letter to the ATypI…
1621.content:
The inclusion of Alexandra Korolkova in the program of ATypI’s conference held in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, between October 28–31, 2026, led to the withdrawal of two Ukrainian speakers. Oleksandra Korchevska-Tsekhosh and Oleksii Chekal, alongside the Ukrainian design community, sent an [open letter](https://en.lb.ua/news/2026/09/08/41322_ukrainian_designers_pull_out.html) to the ATypI Board of Directors requesting Korolkova’s removal. The letter cites Korolkova’s partnership in ParaType and the PT Astra Sans and PT Astra Serif typefaces developed for Astra Linux, used by the Russian military and security services, as justification. According to [TypeDrawers](https://typedrawers.com/discussion/5693/atypi-2026-sharjah-who-is-going), more than three hundred individuals and institutions signed the letter. John Hudson announced that he would not attend because ATypI continued to provide a platform to one of ParaType’s partners. Ongoing discussions under the [#boycottATypI](https://typo.social/tags/boycottATypI) hashtag on Typo.social came back into focus with an [essay](https://monokrom.no/essays/deafening-silence) published shortly before the conference opened. Frode Helland claimed that following the open letter, ATypI deleted critical comments on social media and blocked dissenting voices. An email dated September 19, 2026, informing Korolkova that she was still expected in Sharjah, was later [leaked](https://typo.social/@salnykov/117331087352513046). Helland reported that the board and sponsors remained silent, while public reactions were limited to an [Instagram post](https://www.instagram.com/p/De8s4q9jTVZ/) and a [Mastodon comment](https://typo.social/@stewf@mstdn.party/117485858988413667) stating that participation in the conference was restricted to its Stanford leg.

What the community applauds and what it opposes is also the subject of Agyei Archer’s [article](https://blog.agyei.design/whose-font-is-it-anyway/). Areal, which we introduced in the [August 2025 bulletin](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-b%C3%BClteni-a%C4%9Fustos-2025-410f52e44a70), was developed by redrawing the letterforms from screenshots of an early version of Arial and received positive reactions from the design community. Archer compares the applause for this approach with how the same circle mostly characterizes training artificial intelligence models as *theft*. According to him, ownership is not only about who did the design, but also about against whom and to what extent one can enforce a claim. Furthermore, the license for the free version of Areal prohibits modifying the typeface, creating derivative works, and using it in AI training.

This time, a type foundry takes on the task of explaining the value of licensing. Fontwerk’s article titled [“Why should I pay for fonts?”](https://fontwerk.com/en/text/why-should-i-pay-for-fonts) addresses nine potential objections from managers one by one. It calculates the daily cost of a €3,500 license to be used over five years at approximately €1.90. Drawing on a 2021 study by Neurons and Monotype, it also reports that a well-chosen typeface can boost positive response by up to 13%, memorability by up to 10%, and trust by 9%. It emphasizes that free and open-source typefaces can also be the right choice if they meet requirements. A second article, titled [“Why license fonts?”](https://fontwerk.com/en/text/retail-fonts-vs-free-fonts), presents an eight-point list to convince the team. It highlights GDPR risks that may arise from dynamic font integration in services like Google Fonts, the reduction in distinctiveness from using the same typeface as competitors, the lack of technical support, and viewing typefaces as a mere commodity rather than a strategic brand asset. These discussions also bring the ways licenses are offered to the forefront. Blaze Type’s new subscription model is a concrete example in this regard. In the [Blaze Font Pack](https://blazetype.eu/font-subscription) subscription, licensing is defined via *project slots*. Each slot covers a single client project regardless of duration and number of deliverables, while different projects for the same client require separate slots. Even if the subscription ends, licenses for delivered projects—including websites—remain valid.

The cost of bypassing the production process, however, does not appear on the price tag. LettError’s [article](https://letterror.com/ai) on generative artificial intelligence argues that the design process is not just about producing a result, but also about developing the criteria to evaluate that result. The person engaging in the process weighs alternatives, tests the limits of the tool and the work, and learns to decide what is sufficient. When this process is bypassed, the user fails to develop the criteria needed to judge how good the resulting outcome is. According to the article, the inability to judge the output is the true appeal of these tools, and not learning is where time is saved. If education fails to impart critical thinking skills, reacquiring them later simply by looking at products is nearly impossible.

LettError’s critique linking time savings to a loss of learning also brings the value of time spent on the design process into discussion. Robin Mientjes considers this time as one of the components of design. In her [talk](https://essays.veryrobin.me/modes-of-criticism.html) titled “Modes of Criticism,” introducing Monokrom’s new website, she brings together Simone Weil’s concepts of attention, labor, and rootedness, Walter Benjamin’s question of who writes history, and Francisco Laranjo’s critique of the “It’s nice, that!” mentality. According to Mientjes, care shown to design makes humans more human and can form a stance against hyper-commercialization.

---

1622.title: The Multilingual World of Typography
1622.summary: Monotype and Canva expanded their partnership by adding over a thousand new typeface styles to Canva’s library. This brought the total number of styles on the platform from Monotype and its partner type foundries to over three thousand. According to Monotype’s press release, the expansion focuses on support for…
1622.content:
Monotype and Canva expanded their partnership by adding over a thousand new typeface styles to Canva’s library. This brought the total number of styles on the platform from Monotype and its partner type foundries to over three thousand. According to [Monotype’s press release](https://finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/articles/canva-monotype-bring-1-000-153000540.html), the expansion focuses on support for Arabic, Bengali, Hindi, Khmer, Lao, Thai, and Vietnamese. Meanwhile, TypeTogether released new versions for [Futura®100](https://www.typetogether.com/blog/futura100-a-truly-worldwide-phenomenon) supporting Simplified Chinese, Korean, and nine Indic scripts. Along with last year’s 12 writing systems, the family now reaches 23 writing systems, and according to TypeTogether, more than 90% of the world’s population can use the family in their own language.

On the implementation side, Ritik Shah [compared](https://designregression.com/case%20study/multilingual-directional-signage-in-indian-metros) the directional signage of nine metro systems in India in terms of script hierarchy, alignment, and typeface selection. Six systems use variants of the Devanagari typeface Yogesh dating from the 1980s–1990s, while Nagpur selects Mukta for all writing systems, and Ahmedabad chooses distinct contemporary typefaces per script (Kohinoor, Mukta, Hind). Shah argues that the lack of a standardized guideline leads to a fragmented user experience, proposing legibility testing and script-specific type design work.

The relationship between Indic scripts and digital typography was also on the agenda at [Typoday](https://typoday.org), held in Kochi from September 28–30, 2026. Organized for the 18th time, the conference took place under the theme “Typographic Intersections: Analogue to Digital and Beyond” in collaboration with the IDC School of Design at IIT Bombay. Meanwhile, in a [talk](https://geoffreybawa.com/events/kolam-an-ephemeral-quotodien-ritual-floor-art-as-a-typeface-with-ishan-khosla) delivered in Colombo, Sri Lanka, Ishan Khosla discussed how [The Typecraft Initiative](https://www.typecraftinitiative.org/), of which he is the founder, creates contemporary typefaces rooted in history and tradition alongside craftspeople, indigenous artists, and refugees. Starting from *kolam*, the ancient ritual floor patterns drawn by women on doorsteps, the team worked with 15 kolam artists in Tamil Nadu to develop kolam-based letters.

---

1623.title: Street Letters: Signage, Manhole Covers, and Stone Inscriptions
1623.summary: Jack Usine turns the technical imperfections of his self-taught type design practice into an aesthetic quality. In his interview with Frode Helland, he describes stepping away from commercial graphic design, setting up a studio in rural France, and the interplay between type design and lettering. He explains the…
1623.content:
Jack Usine turns the technical imperfections of his self-taught type design practice into an aesthetic quality. In his [interview](https://monokrom.no/essays/on-resisting-graphic-design) with Frode Helland, he describes stepping away from commercial graphic design, setting up a studio in rural France, and the interplay between type design and lettering. He explains the origin of the [Jules Vernacular](https://vernacular.fr/) archive—which we featured in the [March 2026 bulletin](https://tipografi.substack.com/p/tipografi-bulteni-mart-2026)—through his fascination with poorly made signs and sign painters' failed letterforms. He proposes reading these imperfections as visual poetry by transposing them to different contexts and scales. In the interview, locality and collaboration take precedence over commercial success and designer heroism.

Usine seeing aesthetic possibilities in flawed letterforms also calls to mind another work focusing on the history and transformation of sign painting. In an [interview](https://bl.ag/chatting-with-morgane-come-author-of-la-peinture-en-lettres/), Morgane Côme discusses the preparation process of her book “[La peinture en lettres, Histoire & Renouveau](https://www.lechappee.org/collections/action-graphique/la-peinture-en-lettres),” which examines sign painting in France across the axes of history, technique, and revival, featuring more than five hundred images.

When molds replace the brush, however, letters become anonymous. Maryam Hosseinnia’s [article](https://www.eyemagazine.com/blog/post/farsi-cast-in-iron) examines the Persian lettering on cast-iron manhole covers in Iran in terms of typography, framing, proportion, and contrast. In examples from Tehran, Isfahan, Kashan, and Yazd, the letters range from the most elaborate forms of Nastaliq script to simple shapes that resemble typefaces. On one cover, the dots are unusually large; on some covers, manufacturer names in Latin characters appear alongside the Persian text. The designs of the Isfahan and Kashan covers are inspired by dome architecture, while the raised square grid in Kashan resembles tile patterns.

In contrast to mass-produced typefaces, there are also letters drawn from scratch for a single space. As part of the renovation of the Kloosterkerk in The Hague, LettError [designed](https://letterror.com/articles/kloosterkerk/) a custom inscription on the semicircular Belgian blue stone floor at the entrance, containing the name of the church and a two-line blessing. The inscription was arranged so it can also be read from the exit direction, with the two lines separated by the Chi Rho monogram symbolizing Jesus Christ.

---

1624.title: Small Print
1624.summary: 📦 The Typography Newsletter Archive, where you can search with keywords across the bulletins we have published every month since 2019, is now live! 🔠 Didem Öğmen published design notes for Manchet, which interprets 19th-century extended sans-serif styles. ✨ Microsoft released Michelangelus, a serif typeface inspired…
1624.content:
- 📦 The [Typography Newsletter Archive](https://tipografi-bulteni-arsivi.streamlit.app/), where you can search with keywords across the bulletins we have published every month since 2019, is now live!
- 🔠 Didem Öğmen published design notes for [Manchet](https://journal.didemogmen.com/2026/09/17/background-notes-about-manchet/), which interprets 19th-century extended sans-serif styles.
- ✨ Microsoft released [Michelangelus](https://microsoft.design/articles/designing-michelangelus/), a serif typeface inspired by Michelangelo’s manuscripts.
- 🚀 Designed over more than four years for Arsenal, [Rocastle](https://www.itsnicethat.com/features/david-rudnick-johnnie-campbell-arsenal-rocastle-typeface-graphic-design-spotlight-121026) forms the club's typographic system alongside its Northbank and Chapman typefaces.
- 🧭 Richard Niessen designed a shared visual language based on a line grid for [Kanaalpark](https://dutchdesigndaily.com/stories/kanaalpark/), which runs along the Alkmaar Canal.
- 📚 The sixth issue (F) of [Footnotes](https://fontsinuse.com/uses/80393/footnotes-issue-f) journal, dated September 2026, opens with an article by Sophie Wietlisbach examining Swiss typewriter typefaces through a forensic science lens.
- 📖 Letterform Archive has opened pre-orders for the book on Joan Trochut’s modular type system [SuperTipo Veloz](https://letterformarchive.org/shop/super-veloz/), originally released in 1942.
- 🛠️ [Tegaki](https://tegaki.ink/) is an MIT-licensed open-source library supporting eight writing systems that extracts a typeface’s glyph strokes and stroke order, animating text as if it were being handwritten.
- 📖 TypeMates’ [article](https://www.typemates.com/news/schrift-und-barrierefreiheit) reports that Germany’s Accessibility Strengthening Act (BFSG) does not impose mandatory requirements on typeface selection, while the DIN 1450 standard and DBSV guidelines remain recommendations.
- 🔎 Dan Reynolds [examines](https://www.typeoff.de/2022/12/depesi-types/) the history of Depesi poster typefaces produced in Germany in the early 20th century and the manufacturing technique based on die-cutting vulcanized material and mounting it on wooden blocks.

See you in the next bulletin!

989.title: Scale, AI, and Variable Fonts
989.summary: Monotype announced that its library has reached over 400,000 typeface styles and more than 300 languages. While the company attributes this growth to contributions from more than 5,000 type foundries and an over 75 percent increase in the number of typefaces supporting non-Latin writing systems in 2026, it links the…
989.content:
Monotype [announced](https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-library-reaches-400000-font-styles-expanding-choice-across-languages) that its library has reached over 400,000 typeface styles and more than 300 languages. While the company attributes this growth to contributions from more than 5,000 type foundries and an over 75 percent increase in the number of typefaces supporting non-Latin writing systems in 2026, it links the expansion to the goal of helping brands speak authentically in local markets while maintaining their global identities. Meanwhile, the company’s [partnership](https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-kittl-expand-partnership-bring-brand-typography-to-creative-workflows) with Kittl, launched in 2024, has expanded to encompass enterprise workflows. Monotype customers can now directly access their organizations’ brand typeface libraries from within Kittl’s AI-powered design environment—an access also leveraged beyond designers by marketing teams, agencies, and regional offices. The two companies aim to make it easier for distributed teams to use approved typography and to strengthen brand governance by centralizing typeface licensing and version management.

Distributing an approved typeface to everyone is not enough to deliver the same appearance to everyone. You know that paper, ink, screens, and backgrounds cause the same typeface to be perceived differently. Elliot Jay Stocks, whose piece addressing the optical size debate from a licensing perspective was featured in our [May 2025 bulletin](https://tipografi.substack.com/p/tipografi-bulteni-mays-2026), exemplifies the use of grade to balance these differences in his [article](https://elliotjaystocks.com/blog/keeping-type-consistent). Because grade, unlike weight, allows adjusting perceived darkness without substantially altering the space letters occupy or the text layout, typographic consistency and readability can be preserved across diverse production and display conditions.

While the grade axis strives to keep the space occupied by letters constant, condensed styles deliberately curtail that space. Florian Hardwig chronologically [examines](https://cjtype.com/dunbar-design-repository/articles/on-condensed-geometric-sans-serifs-by-florian-hardwig/) condensed geometric sans serifs from the 1920s to the present through examples such as Kabel, Futura, and Erbar-Grotesk. Explaining that narrow styles are particularly useful in headlines, advertising, and text requiring a compact footprint, the article argues that Dunbar’s narrow, condensed, and compressed widths unite this 1920s heritage with contemporary variable font technology.

Carrying a heritage into variable fonts also requires continuing someone else’s line. [PRINT Magazine](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/gotham-variable-and-the-art-of-evolution/) covered the design process of Gotham Variable—which we announced in our [May 2026 bulletin](https://tipografi.substack.com/p/tipografi-bulteni-mays-2026) as released for Gotham’s 25th anniversary—in an interview with Sara Soskolne. Soskolne explains how she maintained the logic of the original designers while developing new intermediate styles, the limits of her own design autonomy, and the human type designer’s position in the face of AI-assisted production tools. The pre-Now26 interview in which Gotham’s designer Tobias Frere-Jones stated that AI is unnecessary in typography was also featured in our [May 2026 bulletin](https://tipografi.substack.com/p/tipografi-bulteni-mays-2026). As someone else draws new styles today for the family he designed, the question arises of how the boundary between fidelity to the original design and designer autonomy is defined.

---

990.title: From Archive to Matrix, Stone to Sign
990.summary: For anyone seeking to preserve a designer’s logic, the first task is to access the material through which that logic can be traced. Stephen Kelman’s Tschichold Archive project has made accessible 2,184 works from Jan Tschichold’s archive spanning from 1918 to 1974. As Tschichold’s archive becomes navigable, there were…
990.content:
For anyone seeking to preserve a designer’s logic, the first task is to access the material through which that logic can be traced. Stephen Kelman’s [Tschichold Archive](https://tschicholdarchive.com/) project has made accessible 2,184 works from Jan Tschichold’s archive spanning from 1918 to 1974.

As Tschichold’s archive becomes navigable, there were also typefaces in Italy from the same era that the history of typography has largely overlooked. Luca Lattuga’s archival and collection research, conducted over more than a decade, systematically brings together these typefaces produced in Italy’s small print shops and foundries between the 1920s and 1940s in the book [Alfabeti Modernisti Italiani](https://www.oakknoll.com/pages/books/142465/luca-lattuga/alfabeti-modernisti-italiani). Bearing modernist, geometric, decorative, and at times vernacular characteristics, these typefaces reveal an original typographic repertoire when read collectively. CAST Type Foundry, on the other hand, reinterpreted 25 typefaces from the collection unearthed by Lattuga’s research for the digital realm, publishing them as a collection reusable in contemporary graphic design and typography practice under the title [Alfabeti Modernisti Type Specimens](https://www.oakknoll.com/pages/books/142466/cast-cooperativa-anonima-servizi-tipografici/alfabeti-modernisti-type-specimens-ediz-ilusstrata).

Meanwhile, an undigitized branch of the Italian type tradition continues on its path with lead. Preparing printing forms through diverse methods, Dafi Kühne makes extensive use of the Ludlow type casting machine, especially for small point sizes in his posters. Having transported pallet loads of casting matrices belonging to the Nebitype system—produced by the Nebiolo type foundry in Turin and exceptionally rare today—to Switzerland, Kühne is developing a conversion stick with a local machinist to be able to use these original typefaces on the Ludlow. As we learn from Kühne’s [newsletter](https://mailchi.mp/babyinktwice/update-10?e=cd78b8bb64), the designer, who is nearing a solution to the incompatibility between the systems, plans to feature undigitized, original Italian characters in his posters soon. We have previously covered Nebiolo three times in our bulletin. In [May 2022](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-haberleri-may%C4%B1s-2022-c258249bd466), we touched upon an article by Riccardo Olocco analyzing archival materials that survived after Nebiolo’s closure. In [August 2023](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-b%C3%BClteni-a%C4%9Fustos-2023-5ee8b04702ec), we announced the publication of a research book documenting the foundry’s archival, technical, and artistic heritage, and in [October 2025](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-b%C3%BClteni-ekim-2025-803661d110ac), we brought revival discussions into the present through Olocco’s ISType Mono talk. This time, the revival debate continues on a machinist’s workbench.

At the other end of the discussion stands [FH Paragraaf](https://www.typografische.com/typefaces/fh-paragraaf), a serif typeface by [Fatih Hardal](https://www.typografische.com/) that does not adhere strictly to historical models and draws inspiration from the calligraphic roots of Dutch typography. In a process that began in 2020, referencing Hendrik van den Keere’s *Canon Romain* specimen alongside the work of Gerrit Noordzij, Bram de Does, and Jan van Krimpen, the typeface was developed from formal analyses conducted between 2020 and 2026. Reinterpreting the expressive qualities of classical calligraphy for modern publishing and digital rendering, the typeface is a robust text face with its sturdy construction and high legibility…

Does the pen determine the letterform, or the stone? In PampaType’s two-part article, Tere Schultz puts forward a hypothesis regarding the origin of Tuscan letters. The [first part](https://blog.pampatype.com/tuscan-letters-1) extends from 19th-century Tuscan typefaces to Roman epigraphy, discussing previous work by Nicolete Gray and Rob Roy Kelly. Schultz argues that the optical effects created by light, shadow, dust, and erosion on stone-carved inscriptions in cemeteries could make ordinary Roman capitals appear like Tuscan letters, suggesting a potential connection between lapidary inscriptions and Tuscan forms. In the discussion, the *Damasian* or *Philocalian* calligraphy of the 4th-century Roman calligrapher Furius Dionysius Philocalus serves as an early example. The [second part](https://blog.pampatype.com/tuscan-letters-2) brings together vernacular examples extending from Paris to Mexico (specifically Coyoacán), and from Buenos Aires’s “fileteado porteño” tradition to boat lettering in the Brazilian Amazon. This is accompanied by research on the use of Tuscan letters in South America by Priscila Lena Farias and Edna Cunha Lima, as well as the [Floating Letters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZhjOb3JodCU) video project conducted by Fernanda Martins on Amazon boat lettering artisans.

The traces of artisans are sought on land as well. Under the hashtag [#typographictourism](https://www.instagram.com/explore/search/keyword/?q=%23typographictourism), Yorgo Tloupas photographs and archives handmade signboards across regions such as Europe and Mexico. In his article published in [Wallpaper*](https://www.wallpaper.com/design-interiors/corporate-design-branding/typographic-tourism-yorgo-tloupas), he explains how the craft of traditional sign painters declined with the proliferation of personal computers and graphics software, yet original signs still survive in certain cities such as Turin, Genoa, Mérida, and Campeche.

---

991.title: Custom Letters for Identity: Bar, Title Sequence, Sign Language, and Jersey
991.summary: ONBOX studio placed handwriting—which computers had diminished—at the core of visual identity. At an event, the studio had over 100 guests individually handwrite the letters forming the brand name, developing a modular logo from them. It carried the irregular form and texture of the handmade letters across the other…
991.content:
ONBOX studio placed handwriting—which computers had diminished—at the core of visual identity. At an event, the studio had over 100 guests individually handwrite the letters forming the brand name, developing a modular logo from them. It carried the irregular form and texture of the handmade letters across the other identity elements, from menus to coasters, and from signboards to the website. In the article in [PRINT Magazine](https://www.printmag.com/branding-identity-design/bar-supernova-onbox-brand-identity), Adam Hartley of ONBOX explains that in organizing the process, they prioritized authenticity over perfection, balancing the resulting raw energy through the use of typography and whitespace.

If one way to balance raw energy is typography and whitespace, another is not touching it at all. Templo derived the letterforms in DeafCity Hub’s identity from hand gestures in British Sign Language using motion capture technology. By preserving the rough and irregular forms, an authentic character was imparted to the identity. [Creative Boom](https://www.creativeboom.com/news/asking-what-typeface-deafcity-hub-used-for-its-logo-is-the-wrong-question/) notes that due to this approach, asking which typeface was used for the logo is the wrong question.

In contrast to an identity where asking about the typeface is deemed the wrong question, there is also work that turns a logo into a full typeface. Teddy Blanks, co-founder of the studio Chips, shares the background of the title sequence designs he created for films such as Barbie, Weapons, and Werwulf in [an interview](https://www.itsnicethat.com/features/teddy-blanks-chips-film-title-typography-graphic-design-spotlight-240826). He relates that he redrew the Barbie logo using high-resolution images sourced from a late-1980s magazine into a complete font, and developed a typeface inspired by a 14th-century manuscript for Werwulf. The interview also explores how typographic decisions in projects such as The Green Knight and Nickel Boys establish connections with the film narrative.

While on film the letter serves the narrative, on the back of a jersey the letter must first be legible from across the pitch. Developed by [Fatih Hardal](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcgYZysjALn/) for Beerschot jerseys as part of Nova’s evolving visual language, the name and number design presents a distinctive character with its proportions, weight, chamfered corners, and rounded details. The design strikes a balanced relationship between long-distance legibility on the pitch and Nova’s distinctive character.

One way to extend this balance established on the back of a jersey across an entire club identity is assigning roles to letters. Milan-based Alkemy+ developed a new brand strategy and visual identity system for Palermo FC based on a listening process lasting over a year. As reported by [The Brand Identity](https://the-brandidentity.com/project/over-a-year-of-listening-shaped-alkemy-s-identity-for-palermo-fc), the club’s existing crest and pink-and-black colors were retained. The Palermo Mosaico family, forming the typographic core of the project, was drawn divided into three roles under the design direction of Guido Scolaro and Andrea Biggio. Mosaico Serif assumes the symbolic role, *Mosaico Flare* the editorial and display role, and *Mosaico Sans* the system layer. While Rosa Palermo was retained as a fixed reference point in the color palette, colors derived from the city—such as Blu Mediterraneo, Verde Favorita, Oro Barocco, and Marmo Siciliano—were added to the system. In our article [“Letters on the Pitch”](https://medium.com/tipografi/sahadaki-harfler-spor-markalamas%C4%B1nda-tipografinin-y%C3%BCkselen-g%C3%BCc%C3%BC-8f249d1300ad) published in 2025, we touched upon the aesthetic and symbolic value gained by clubs establishing identities through custom typefaces. Unfortunately, despite the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) lifting the mandatory Arial requirement, no similar moves have come from clubs in Turkey.

---

992.title: Small Points
992.summary: 📚 Slanted Publishers has released the book Slanted Experimental Type 4.0, produced with students from the Dortmund University of Applied Sciences and Arts. 🖋️ Opened on September 19, 2026, at the Nilüfer Municipality Literature Museum, the exhibition “The Journey of the Pen” brings the history of writing and…
992.content:
📚 Slanted Publishers has released the book [Slanted Experimental Type 4.0](https://www.slanted.de/product/slanted-experimental-type-4-0/), produced with students from the Dortmund University of Applied Sciences and Arts.

🖋️ Opened on September 19, 2026, at the Nilüfer Municipality Literature Museum, the exhibition “[The Journey of the Pen](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdLwtAaMOmA/)” brings the history of writing and pens—stretching from wall paintings and cuneiform to the digital age—to visitors through examples compiled by poet, writer, and editor C. Hakkı Zariç from pens in the museum collection, running until March 20, 2027.

🎉 Organizing typography-focused events in Toronto since 2014, [Swash & Serif](https://swashandserif.ca) has transformed its tenth edition into a month-long festival program. The program kicks off on October 15, 2026, with the lettering competition *League of Letters*, and continues with an exhibition opening at the Northern Contemporary Gallery between November 12–17, 2026, followed by a typography conference on November 20, 2026.

🎓 [TypeParis](https://typeparis.com/spring27) is moving its type design program from Paris to the island of Menorca, Spain. Applications can be submitted until January 14, 2027, for the three-week TypeParis Spring 27 program to be held between April 5–24, 2027, offered at two levels: Foundation for those taking their first steps into type design, and Expert for experienced type designers.

See you in the next bulletin!

1004.title: Platforms, Ownership, and the Economics of Type
1004.summary: Monotype has brought the MyFonts app to the ChatGPT platform, embedding font discovery directly into the chat interface. Currently launched in the US market, the app allows users to receive font recommendations in English conversations by using the @MyFonts command. It is worth noting that turning the catalog search…
1004.content:
Monotype has brought the MyFonts app to the ChatGPT platform, [embedding](https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-launches-myfonts-app-chatgpt-bringing-real-font-discovery-ai) font discovery directly into the chat interface. Currently launched in the US market, the app allows users to receive font recommendations in English conversations by using the *@MyFonts* command. It is worth noting that turning the catalog search experience into a recommendation engine obscures the editorial layer of font selection, as which target audience, commercial priority, or dataset shapes the recommendation remains outside the interface.

TypeToday's interview with Sam Berlow [looks](https://type.today/en/journal/thetypefounders) at the type industry from a different angle. Proposing a model that acquires designers' intellectual property and assumes commercial and marketing operations, The Type Founders allows designers to focus solely on designing type. Featuring designers such as Mark Simonson and Matthew Carter, the model positions itself against Monotype on the premise that selling the foundry is not the only way out. While easing designers' operational burden is advantageous, transferring intellectual property may not be easily embraced by type designers. Consequently, designers' willingness to participate will determine the sustainability of the model.

A bill debated in the Colorado Senate puts forward a more technical proposal on how creative property can be protected within a corporate structure. The [Artist Corporation](https://www.artistcorporations.com/), or A-Corp model, mandates that at least 51 percent of voting shares remain with the artist. In the event of dissolution, returning intellectual property to the creator rather than transferring it to investors could provide robust protection for enduring assets such as type families. This framework relies on contractual architecture rather than a romantic promise of independence. The goal is to explicitly define which party retains decision-making authority while capital is being provided.

The fact that [Fontdue](https://www.fontdue.com/) has served more than 100 type foundries since 2018 is another data point reminding us that independent font sales are still seeking their own infrastructure. The platform enables type foundries to manage sales, licensing, and checkout flows through their own domain names. Dinamo consolidating its publications onto a single website can likewise be [read](https://editions.abcdinamo.com/) in a similar light. Type foundries no longer merely distribute font files; they are also establishing their own publishing and information architectures.

---

1005.title: Labels, Artificial Intelligence, and Visual Authority
1005.summary: Elizabeth Goodspeed examines the growing prevalence of the question "What aesthetic is this?" through the lens of algorithmic classification culture. Grouping images under the same label based on visual similarities, divorced from their historical, social, and material contexts, is not an innocent classification…
1005.content:
Elizabeth Goodspeed [examines](https://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/elizabeth-goodspeed-whats-in-a-name-categorising-aesthetics-creative-industry-190526) the growing prevalence of the question "What aesthetic is this?" through the lens of algorithmic classification culture. Grouping images under the same label based on visual similarities, divorced from their historical, social, and material contexts, is not an innocent classification practice. Goodspeed emphasizes that naming has become an act of establishing cultural authority rather than merely being descriptive, and that whoever first coins a label can rise to the position of a cultural commentator without having produced anything. Trend-forecasting companies, in turn, directly convert this informal cultural capital into a commercial product.

AI companies turning to serif typefaces represents the more corporate side of this same representational economy. The preference of brands like Claude and Manus for serif typefaces is [associated](https://www.wired.com/story/ai-has-come-for-serif-fonts/) by critics with the concept of *tasteslop*, which signifies an effort to project a facade of artificial refinement. According to San Francisco-based designer Keya Vadgama, this choice is a strategy to signal humanity in order to gloss over artificial intelligence's inherently cold and impersonal nature; after all, the calligraphically rooted essence of serif typefaces makes them more fluid and human. When prompted to explain its own design choices, Claude explains this trend through the pursuit of trust, authority, and literary gravitas. The choice of letterforms here is not merely a visual decision; it is a declaration of which cultural memory the tech company wishes to align itself with. That is why Vadgama's remark resonates so well: "Even if you use Comic Sans, you’re still an AI company." Typefaces can soften the chill, but they cannot change what you are.

---

1006.title: Archives, Street Lettering, and the Material History of the Letter
1006.summary: "Signs are actors. Some are wallflowers, barely speaking above a whisper, while others shout and flirt, beckoning for attention." — E. Goodspeed Goodspeed re-examines Ed Ruscha's photographic archive of Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, spanning from 1966 to 2007, from a typographic perspective. Ranging from neon signs…
1006.content:
> "Signs are actors. Some are wallflowers, barely speaking above a whisper, while others shout and flirt, beckoning for attention."
>
> — E. Goodspeed

Goodspeed [re-examines](https://www.sunsetoversunset.org/stories/signs) Ed Ruscha's photographic archive of Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, spanning from 1966 to 2007, from a typographic perspective. Ranging from neon signs and hand-painted lettering to psychedelic 1970s letterforms and corporate brand identities, this visual history demonstrates through concrete examples how each era inscribed its cultural priorities and production technologies into the form of letters.

Arno Verweij's [Amsterdam Typography](https://www.amsterdamtypography.nl/) and [Netherlands Typography](https://www.netherlandstypography.nl/) archives [document](https://bl.ag/amsterdam-lettering-and-typography-through-the-ages/) the same domain in a more systematic manner. Having accumulated over 4,000 photographs across the two sites since 2019, the archive—together with a special 1,850-image section curated from the City Archives' digital image bank for Amsterdam's 750th anniversary—extends its earliest examples back to 1857. This visual continuity, reaching from an 1877 painted wall advertisement to the curly calligraphic letters (*krulletters*) of 1958, shows that vernacular typography can only be fully comprehended through a sustained and patient archival practice.

While sign painting is often described as a lost or nostalgic trade, Nan Parati hand-lettering more than 3,000 signs each year in New Orleans [stands as a rebuttal](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/legendary-jazz-fest-sign-writer-nan-parati-makes-music-with-her-lettering/?mc_cid=915924123f&mc_eid=48a95a3cf1) to this assumption. Having prepared the signs for Jazz Fest for 42 years, Parati almost single-handedly carries the memory of the festival's typography through her personal styles named *Fun Times Roman* and *Nanuscript*. The fact that young sign painters are recirculating this craft through workshops, communities like [Burds of the Brush](https://medium.com/tipografi/burds-of-the-brush-dayan%C4%B1%C5%9Fmayla-b%C3%BCy%C3%BCyen-bir-topluluk-a206f7cce6d5), and independent work shows that street lettering continues to thrive not only in archives, but also on the workbench.

News of Gençlerbirliği from Turkey offers an apt example of the intersection between urban identity and sports. According to information shared by [Yaşar Soylu](https://x.com/yasarsoyluuu/status/2067261648532840822?s=20) from TRT Spor, the club will use Oğuzhan Cengiz's Ankara typeface on its new-season jerseys. The typeface won first prize in the font category of a competition launched by the Ankara Metropolitan Municipality in 2021. Thus, a typeface designed for public signage gains visibility on the football jersey of the very same city. This development operates differently from custom-commissioned typefaces: here, the city embraces the typeface first, and the team subsequently adopts it. We previously shared these developments with our readers in our [May](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-haberleri-mayıs-2021-d8cf2966d3ea) and [August](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-haberleri-a%C4%9Fustos-2021-b87f55e89171) 2021 bulletins. The examples examined in our article titled "[Letters on the Pitch](https://medium.com/tipografi/sahadaki-harfler-spor-markalamas%C4%B1nda-tipografinin-y%C3%BCkselen-g%C3%BCc%C3%BC-8f249d1300ad)" analyzed custom typefaces commissioned for clubs. The relationship urban typography establishes with brand identity was also opened for discussion at the panel "[From City to Brand: Sakarya](https://www.satso.org.tr/komitehaber/20621/satso-12--meslek-komitesi-ve-ared-is-birligindeki-etkinlik-sektor-paydaslarini-bir-araya-getirdi.aspx)" held on June 16, 2026. During the panel, one of our editors, Murat Ertürk, discussed how signage and vernacular lettering styles shaped Sakarya's visual identity through his book "[Letters of Sakarya](https://www.muraterturk.com/book.html)". This example serves as a reminder that vernacular typography is not merely archival material belonging to the past, but an active layer still operating in how cities define, remember, and brand themselves.

There is also significant activity on the archival desk. Eve Scarborough of Letterform Archive [reports](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-emigre-font-development-files/) that the digitization of Emigre's font development files has made the early digital typography production processes of the 1980s and 1990s far more legible. Proof prints, handwritten corrections, correspondence, and reference materials document a design culture where analog and digital production were not divorced from one another, but rather intertwined on the very same workspace.

A video investigating the origins of Lorem Ipsum [distances itself](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kL1PDqzqhM4) from the widespread assumption that the text has been handed down unchanged since the 1500s. It explains that the form in use today was standardized especially during the 20th century within Letraset and modern typesetting culture, while its roots trace back to Cicero's classical Latin texts. Jeff Jarvis's forthcoming book "[Hot Type](https://www.publishersweekly.com/9798765123959)", to be published in the coming months by Bloomsbury Academic, similarly addresses typesetting technology alongside media history, examining how the Linotype machine transformed the newspaper, book, and magazine industries through the lens of the birth of mass communication.

At Commercial Type, Paul Barnes's Action Grotesque [article](https://commercialtype.com/about/collections/action_grotesque) recalls Walter Tracy's *Adsans* and *Doric* typefaces designed for Linotype alongside Harry Carter's principles of optical adjustment. The way Van Blokland's function-first approach for text sizes transforms into an unexpected character at display sizes effectively demonstrates that optical scaling is far more than dry mathematics.

---

1007.content:

🎥 Session recordings from TypeLab 2026, held as part of the Typographics Festival on [24](https://www.youtube.com/live/UR4zw3VOWwU?si=-Xq3kImPDljO4TMv) and [25 June](https://www.youtube.com/live/hwENpN6W8qM?si=tngXsyfYyFpRJ5US), have been made available on YouTube.

⚔️ [Coding Font](https://www.codingfont.com/) offers a tournament-style elimination experience comparing programming fonts through head-to-head matchups.

🌍 Rosetta Type's [Hyperglot](https://hyperglot.rosettatype.com/checker) tool analyzes which languages an uploaded font supports.

✨ Oğuzhan Cengiz announced his new typeface named [Pecal](https://www.myfonts.com/collections/pecal-font-hurufatfont-type-foundry?queryId=ac50a0e075431a55176f25b4f1e039e2&index=universal_search_data&objectIDs=MTE2OTc3NF81NTE3MzlfMTc4MTY5NDUxNA), which unites humanist, geometric, and grotesque sans serif traditions within a single system.

🧪 Robert Finke's [User Type Lab](https://makertube.net/w/e6mPnmauoRn4r7mS7shzDM) project introduces measurable feedback into the type design process by subjecting letterforms to A/B testing with users.

993.title: Revival Criticism, Historical Archives, and Vernacular Sources
993.summary: In her essay critiquing revival practices in type design, Robin Mientjes emphasizes that reproducing past designs often fosters an excessive attachment to specific names and examples rather than an understanding of design principles. According to Mientjes, the true value of historical material lies not in imitating…
993.content:
In her [essay](https://essays.veryrobin.me/reconsidering-revivals.html) critiquing revival practices in type design, Robin Mientjes emphasizes that reproducing past designs often fosters an excessive attachment to specific names and examples rather than an understanding of design principles. According to Mientjes, the true value of historical material lies not in imitating forms, but in comprehending its underlying logic, the conditions of its era, and principles of craftsmanship.

Cambridge University Library's project presents a concrete example of facilitating access to historical material. Donated to the university in 1953 by the Deberny & Peignot Type Foundry, more than three thousand punches by John Baskerville have been analyzed using advanced imaging techniques and [made accessible online](https://cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/collections/baskervillepunches/2). Doug Wilson's [research](https://buttondown.com/linotypebook/archive/smithsonian-discoveries/) shares the same methodological priority. Sifting through the Linotype Company archives for the book he is preparing, Wilson worked with 34 boxes of archival material, rare publications, and graphic arts collections.

In contrast to Wilson's research grounded in corporate archives, Pooja Saxena archives dozens of writing systems across India through the [India Street Lettering](https://indiastreetlettering.com) project, categorizing them by style, material, and function. One of the project's outputs, the [book](https://indiastreetlettering.com/india-street-lettering-a-journey-through-typographic-craft-culture/), brings together more than 300 photographs compiled from 17 cities and 13 writing systems. Jack Usine's [Jules Vernacular](https://vernacular.fr) archive offers a European counterpart to this systematic documentation approach, featuring over 1,700 photographs from across France.

The reflection of documentation practices in type design often stems from the designer's relationship with the local environment. Two recently released typefaces stand out as tangible examples of this relationship: [Cassis](https://frerejones.com/blog/cassis-generous-geometry), designed by Nina Stössinger inspired by Swiss and Belgian street signage, and [Buckridge](https://djr.com/notes/buckridge-font-of-the-month), developed by David Jonathan Ross based on lettering from an old trigonometry textbook. In an [interview](https://maketypework.com/making-type-amy-hood-of-hoodzpah/), Amy Hood also explained how she designs typefaces drawing from Southern California's historic signage and *Midcentury* aesthetics, noting that deciding when to finish is the most challenging stage in every project.

Beyond the relationship established with the local, the issue of ownership addressed in Samaa Khullar's article is also noteworthy. In her [article](https://www.gqmiddleeast.com/article/the-designer-behind-mamdanis-arabic-campaign-has-a-bigger-vision) centered on the visual identity of Zohran Mamdani's Arabic election campaign, Khullar demonstrates that from the invention of the printing press to keyboards and digital typefaces, technology has consistently tended to simplify writing systems and strip them of their nuances, and that Arab designers are fighting to reclaim their own writing systems.

---

994.title: Type Design as Corporate Identity, Context, and Mode of Expression
994.summary: Designed for Snickers, Snickers Sans is a current example of how brand typography can transform into a functional system. Derived from the brand's iconic logo, the type family brings the American Gothic tradition into the brand identity. Commissioned by Swedish dairy company Arla for use across more than 120 markets…
994.content:
Designed for Snickers, [Snickers Sans](https://studio-drama.com/projects/snickers) is a current example of how brand typography can transform into a functional system. Derived from the brand's iconic logo, the type family brings the American Gothic tradition into the brand identity. Commissioned by Swedish dairy company Arla for use across more than 120 markets and millions of packaging units, [Arla Smile](https://capdesign.se/arla-smile-ett-typsnitt-designat-for-varlden/) stands out with rounded forms and pronounced ink traps that enhance legibility. Both projects demonstrate that type design is the product of functional requirements such as scalability, multilingual support, and corporate consistency.

Monotype made headlines with two separate announcements this month. Thanks to a partnership with brand management platform Frontify, typefaces in the Monotype Fonts library can now be accessed directly within Frontify, allowing creative teams to [manage](https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-and-frontify-streamline-workflows-font-integration) brand typography without switching platforms. In addition, the company launched its [AI Search](https://www.monotype.com/company/press-release/monotype-launches-ai-search-transforming-font-search-and-discovery-conversational-ai) tool, powered by natural language and conversational AI. Allowing users to search using phrases describing mood, brand character, or context of use, the system aims to redefine font discovery by moving away from traditional search methods.

A compelling addition was made to typographic applications in the public sphere this month. Excerpts from Obama's 2015 "You Are America" speech were rendered in the Gotham typeface on the facade of the [Obama Presidential Center](https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/03/07/obama-presidential-center-opening-juneteenth-chicago) in Chicago, scheduled to open on June 19, 2026. We previously saw a similar example at the [University of Amsterdam Library](https://letterror.com/uva/index.html), where translations of a line by Martinus Nijhoff across 23 languages and 6 writing systems were inscribed on the library facade using a custom typeface designed specifically for the building by Erik van Blokland. Although both projects establish the relationship between architecture and typography differently, the typeface choices are not accidental; they are deliberate decisions consistent with each structure's public discourse.

In an interview with Monotype Creative Director Charles Nix, the role of typography in branding systems was [discussed](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/typography-and-the-future-of-olympic-branding/) through the lens of the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics visual identity. According to Nix, the challenge is not designing a good logo, but building a robust system where even small elements—such as colors, symbols, or typographic details—can evoke the whole. The question of how local references transform into a distinctive voice and remain meaningful without falling into imitation forms the focal point of the conversation.

Neville Brody's release of the [Popaganda](https://typenetwork.com/articles/popaganda-interview-giveaway) typeface as an expanded family represents a different stance. In an interview with Lucas Czarnecki, Brody noted that this typeface, drawing from reggae record labels and the agitprop tradition, was designed as an intentional tool of friction against today's notion of flawless typography. This attitude aligns with the argument formulated by Agyei Archer in his recent [article](https://blog.agyei.design/why-you-should-release-that-shitty/). Archer emphasized that the backlash against the sterile aesthetic created by AI and corporate technology is driving demand for imperfect yet characterful typefaces.

---

995.title: Digital Infrastructure: CSS Conventions, Security, and Tools
995.summary: Alex Kladov highlighted the text-wrap: pretty property, explaining ways to preserve paragraph integrity and achieve more balanced line breaks in web typography. This approach aims to reduce single-word final lines and produce more balanced text blocks by re-evaluating the closing portion of a paragraph. Meanwhile, the…
995.content:
Alex Kladov highlighted the *text-wrap: pretty* property, [explaining](https://webkit.org/blog/16547/better-typography-with-text-wrap-pretty/) ways to preserve paragraph integrity and achieve more balanced line breaks in web typography. This approach aims to reduce single-word final lines and produce more balanced text blocks by re-evaluating the closing portion of a paragraph. Meanwhile, the [tool](https://clagnut.com/sandbox/font-size-adjust.html) developed by Richard Rutter helps resolve visual inconsistencies arising from metric differences between fonts—such as x-height—using the *font-size-adjust* property.

Concurrently with these technical developments, the dimension of security was also brought to the fore. Paul Wood [analyzed](https://paultendo.github.io/posts/confusable-vision-visual-similarity/) 1,418 character pairs from Unicode's list of confusable characters at the pixel level across 230 system fonts. Finding that 96.5 percent of the pairs posed no visual threat, Wood determined that 82 pairs overlapped identically with Latin letters in at least one font. In this respect, the study demonstrates that confusability from a typographic perspective is not merely a character trait, and that typeface choice serves as a decisive factor, turning font selection directly into a security decision.

Software developer McCloskey [explained](https://mccloskeybr.com/articles/font_rendering.html) the computational pipeline extending from font files to pixel generation. Detailing why the *Signed Distance Fields* technique yields sharper results at every size and resolution, McCloskey demonstrates within a technical framework that typographic success in digital media depends not only on aesthetic choices, but also on the mathematical interpretation capabilities of display technologies.

This technical reality imposed by screen technologies intersects with the search for organic forms and the material production challenges faced by designers translating traditional practices into the digital sphere. Type designer John Roshell [recounted](https://adobe.design/stories/community/making-type-john-roshell-of-comicraft-swell-type) the process of bringing comic book lettering into the digital age. He emphasized having to design typefaces from scratch to bring computer-idealized geometric forms closer to the organic structure of handwritten characters, and that the time pressure of that era shaped both his productivity and expertise. Meanwhile, a [short documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGihdIyEHZI) produced about [House Industries](https://houseindustries.com/) founder Andy Cruz centers on the financial realities of the studio's founding period. Cruz shared that he had to sell his Porsche 944 Turbo to fund technical equipment, illustrating the economic reality of design practice through a personal example.
