997.title: Artificial Intelligence, Surveillance, and Typography
997.summary: Designed by Parker Jones and Rajshree Saraf, Hellcare Regular turns the rejection of legibility into a conscious typographic strategy. Taking the illegibility of doctors' handwriting as its reference, the font translates the bureaucratic and inaccessible structure of the American healthcare system into a visual…
997.content:
Designed by Parker Jones and Rajshree Saraf, [Hellcare Regular](https://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/parker-jones-rajshree-saraf-hellcare-regular-graphic-design-project-130526) turns the rejection of legibility into a conscious typographic strategy. Taking the illegibility of doctors' handwriting as its reference, the font translates the bureaucratic and inaccessible structure of the American healthcare system into a visual language. The complex medical documents and forms of communication Jones encountered during his father's cancer treatment form the starting point of the font. The formal distortion is essentially a critique of the alienation generated by the healthcare system.

This approach also recalls a broader tradition in which legibility is not seen as an absolute value in typography. At the Letterform Archive, as [recounted by Zachary Sauer](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/), Wolfgang Weingart (1941–2021) developed a practice that challenged the Swiss typographic tradition from within rather than outright rejecting it, pushing the limits of modernist order through his *Typografische Monatsblätter* covers and photomechanical experiments. Both approaches demonstrate typography's power as a critical and political form of expression.

Oliver Schöndorfer [explains](https://pimpmytype.com/about-ai-design/) through the lens of AI why these approaches are even more important today. According to Schöndorfer, while typography can transform mediocre output into intentional design, establish visual hierarchy, and lend a distinctive character to a project, AI detaches the designer from thinking, and the real danger is not speed but the atrophy of judgment… [Nick Shinn](https://ilovetypography.com/2026/05/13/font-faces-nick-shinn/) stands on similar ground. Stating that drawing is a cognitive process distinct from machine learning, Shinn argues that this organic structure, grounded in muscle memory and cultural intelligence, forms an ontological barrier against artificial intelligence. Tobias Frere-Jones, in his [interview](https://typeparis.com/news/q-a-tobias-frere-jones) published ahead of the [Now26](https://typeparis.com/now26) conference, similarly remarks that AI creates an unnecessary workload in typography, while expressing that Google Fonts has had an *erosive* effect on the traditional Western market.

---

998.title: The Material Layers of History
998.summary: A critique of technology inevitably invites a confrontation with history. Lukas Paltram of Dalton Maag argues that returning to physical sources is essential to reinterpreting typography, emphasizing that the original qualities of metal typefaces on paper were largely lost during the early digitization era. As part of…
998.content:
A critique of technology inevitably invites a confrontation with history. Lukas Paltram of Dalton Maag [argues](https://www.daltonmaag.com/resources/blog/2026-03-23-recasting-the-past.html) that returning to physical sources is essential to reinterpreting typography, emphasizing that the original qualities of metal typefaces on paper were largely lost during the early digitization era. As part of *The Recast Collection*, the type foundry bypasses digital files to work directly from original printed specimens, sketch drawings, and type specimens in archives. *Versum Recast*, one of the collection's members to be released in 2026, reinterprets Adrian Frutiger's 1957 neo-grotesque system as a three-axis variable font.

The return to physical sources also prepares the ground for rethinking typography's historical processes. Étienne Ghys [examines](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1OIxzewWilc) how letter anatomy was constructed along a trajectory stretching from Gutenberg to Luca Pacioli and Albrecht Dürer's quest for geometric proportions, and onward to Donald Knuth's Metafont system. According to Ghys, typefaces are not merely vessels for conveying information; they are structures that represent power, transmit cultural memory, and shape visual perception. The transition from traditional craftsmanship to Bézier curves is therefore not merely a technical transformation, but a historical rupture that altered how letterforms are perceived…

The labor dimension of typography's history, which often remains in the background, becomes visible in an [essay](https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/twilight-of-the-velocipede/) adapted from Alex Wright's book "[Empire of Ink](https://alexwright.com/books/empire-of-ink/)". In the 1870s, before the Linotype had entered the scene, compositors known as *Swifts*—capable of typesetting roughly 760 words per hour—drew crowds of thousands into halls for typesetting competitions. Beyond demonstrations of technical skill, these exhibitions were public arenas where female compositors waged union struggles. The refusal of organizers to recognize the results of women who outperformed their male competitors in an 1886 competition demonstrates that the history of typography cannot be explained through a purely technological narrative.

Another trajectory of this historical layer extending to the present day is opened up by the research of Borna Izadpanah and Onur Yazıcıgil. The article titled "[Crafting Global Typography: Origins, Dissemination, and Adaptation of Naskh Types from Istanbul](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-royal-asiatic-society/article/crafting-global-typography-origins-dissemination-and-adaptation-of-naskh-types-from-istanbul/8B34BD1F60DD72A19497D4A5523D82BF)" investigates the global circulation and geographical transformations of the 24-point Ottoman Naskh printing types developed in 1867 by Ottoman-Armenian punchcutter Oḥannes Mühendisyan and court calligrapher Mustafa İzzet Efendi. While bringing to light a vital lineage of production sidelined by Western-centric typographic historiography, the study reminds us that typography must also be read across the dimensions of cultural circulation, labor, and political representation, far beyond formal matters alone.

---

999.title: Licensing, Privacy, and the Cost of Free
999.summary: Jürgen Siebert and Ivo Gabrowitsch directly address the issue of typographic monoculture caused by free typeface services like Google Fonts. The adoption of Roboto and Open Sans by millions of companies creates an effect of invisibility that progressively erodes distinctiveness in digital environments. According to…
999.content:
Jürgen Siebert and Ivo Gabrowitsch directly [address](https://fontwerk.com/en/text/retail-fonts-vs-free-fonts) the issue of typographic monoculture caused by free typeface services like Google Fonts. The adoption of Roboto and Open Sans by millions of companies creates an effect of invisibility that progressively erodes distinctiveness in digital environments. According to the authors, free typefaces carry severe limitations in technical support, long-term maintenance, language coverage, and brand authenticity. The legal dimension of this debate came to the fore when integrating the Google Fonts infrastructure into websites via an external API resulted in visitors' IP addresses and browser data being transmitted to corporate servers without consent. A 2022 ruling by a Munich court defined this data flow as a clear violation of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), compelling website administrators to host typefaces on local servers. It remains difficult to know how many websites still operate in ignorance of this ruling. Moreover, because scanning local typeface directories on user devices plays a uniquely identifying role in browser fingerprinting, digital typography also turns into a data security concern.

Against this backdrop, new structures supporting independent type foundries are taking shape. Developed by [NaN Type Foundry](https://www.nan.xyz/), [fonts.xyz](https://www.fonts.xyz/) has been announced as a new platform bringing independent type foundries together under one roof. The platform's most notable feature is a single license model covering print, web, app, advertising, and social media use. Promising to pay designers 80% of sales in royalties, the platform also offers the possibility of building foundry-specific websites. As in all platform economies, whether this model is genuinely sustainable will only become apparent through long-term distribution and revenue practices.

Elliot Jay Stocks [connects](https://adobe.design/ideas/the-old-typography-is-new-again) the optical size discussion to the licensing agenda from a different angle. He notes that glyphs, which were designed separately for small and large point sizes during the era of movable type, have regained significance in the digital environment thanks to variable font technology. Design applications and browsers can adapt letterforms automatically or manually according to font size, making typography more responsive to context. This technical flexibility also highlights the difference between free typefaces that offer limited axes and features and advanced variable font systems.

Type.today published an in-depth [interview](https://type.today/en/journal/bulac) with Benjamin Guichard, scientific director of the Paris-based library [BULAC](https://www.bulac.fr/), on non-Western writing systems. With its extensive collection, BULAC hosts research projects ranging from developing machine learning models for Arabic manuscripts to designing fictional writing systems with students from École Estienne. The interview discusses why type designers and libraries need each other and what an independent library focused on non-Western publications means today. It serves as a reminder of how little documented the intersection of type design and library practice remains.

---

1001.title: Licensing Complexity and Market Behavior
1001.summary: The results of the survey, conducted by Fontstand throughout 2025 and answered by over 1,300 respondents, turned a long-debated tension in the type industry into concrete data. 93.8% of participants prefer one-time purchases over subscription models, citing the ability to re-access files in long-term projects and…
1001.content:
The [results of the survey,](https://fontstand.com/news/design-news/survey/) conducted by Fontstand throughout 2025 and answered by over 1,300 respondents, turned a long-debated tension in the type industry into concrete data. 93.8% of participants prefer one-time purchases over subscription models, citing the ability to re-access files in long-term projects and avoid losing access when a license expires. While Adobe Fonts maintains its dominant position in subscription usage because it is bundled with the Creative Cloud subscription, this rate drops to 8.8% when it comes to conscious choice.

Behind this pattern of preference lies a structural problem with the licensing system. Nearly two-thirds of respondents state that they have abandoned purchasing a typeface at least once due to complex or ambiguous terms. The most frequently voiced complaint is the requirement for distinct licenses across web, print, and application uses. Designers note turning to Google Fonts to avoid the difficulty of explaining these distinctions during client meetings. These numbers clearly demonstrate that lost revenue stems not from price, but from confusion. While design quality leads typeface selection at 94%, clear licensing follows closely at 59% when asked about expectations from subscription services, right behind affordable pricing at 64%.

In an environment where the licensing system so heavily constrains user decisions, Latinotype's release of Willy Caslon brings a different question to the fore. When expectations for quality and functionality rise, must revival projects adapt as well? [According to Ameel Khan's review,](https://www.insanityworks.org/randomtangent/2026/4/12/willy-caslon-an-excellent-caslon-revival) this work resolves the imbalances inherited from the original movable type era—which the vast majority of existing digital versions of Caslon deliberately preserve—making the typeface more functional in modern publishing contexts.

---

1002.title: Technical and Conceptual Boundaries of Variable Fonts
1002.summary: Current discussions around variable fonts are no longer confined to the expansion of technical capacity, increasingly moving toward a multi-layered ground encompassing aesthetic, theoretical, and industrial dimensions. Aleksandra Samuļenkova's article examining six projects within the context of the TDC72 Typeface…
1002.content:
Current discussions around variable fonts are no longer confined to the expansion of technical capacity, increasingly moving toward a multi-layered ground encompassing aesthetic, theoretical, and industrial dimensions. Aleksandra Samuļenkova's [article](https://tdc.org/news/movement-matters-variable-fonts-new-tonal-expressions/) examining six projects within the context of the TDC72 Typeface Design Competition that transform the variable font beyond technical flexibility into an expressive medium where motion is woven into the essence of the design, alongside Contrast Foundry's [article](https://contrastfoundry.com/projects/how-to-design-a-variable-font) exploring unconventional axis uses—such as stencil effects, motion simulation, and pattern-based experiments in addition to classical axes like weight, width, and slant—materialize the creative possibilities of the variable font format, offering a powerful reference for both type designers and designers closely following this technology. These developments find concrete reflection in applications demonstrating how variable fonts redefine the balance between legibility and flexibility in large-scale system design, as seen in the [Monaspace](https://lettermatic.com/custom/monaspace-case-study) project developed in collaboration between Lettermatic and GitHub. While providing flexibility along weight, width, and slant axes, Monaspace aims to resolve legibility issues inherent to monospace typefaces through an approach dubbed *Texture Healing*.

When the debate descends to the interface level, Michael Rafailyk, in his critique of the Liquid Glass design language, [argues](https://michaelrafailyk.com/blog/liquidglassfromatypographyperspective) that the optical size principle has not sufficiently translated into interface design, and that while glass material succeeds on large surfaces, it creates contrast and clarity issues in small-scale icons. As a solution, he suggests designing icons with scale-sensitive variations, parallel to the logic of optical size in variable fonts.

---

1003.title: Research, History, and Identity: Typography's Theoretical Ground
1003.summary: Typotheque, as a type foundry with a full-time scientist on staff, is currently conducting three distinct research studies simultaneously. Aiming to rank the foundry's catalog through crowdsourced participation, the Font Expressiveness Game presents users with pairs of typefaces and asks which feels more expressive. A…
1003.content:
Typotheque, as a type foundry with a full-time scientist on staff, is currently conducting three distinct research studies simultaneously. Aiming to rank the foundry's catalog through crowdsourced participation, the [Font Expressiveness Game](https://typotheque.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_1T6LwPLfIeIdzsG?utm_source=newsletter_155&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=2026-03-25&utm_content=FontExpressivenessGame) presents users with pairs of typefaces and asks which feels more expressive. A field study conducted in Hyderabad in collaboration with Urdu University and the Center for Urdu Language [investigates](https://typotheque.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_dd0PEgjOynP5kaO) how different Nastaliq styles are perceived by readers of Urdu, Arabic, and Persian. A [survey](https://typotheque.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_3rX0mXjScVJsrKS) exploring user preferences and needs regarding accessibility in design, in collaboration with Matthew Baxter, is also ongoing. Participation in all three surveys remains open.

Alongside this landscape of current perception research, Sara Rosinsky examines an overlooked relic of printing history. Because Linotype typesetting machines lacked a delete function, operators would run their fingers down the first two vertical columns of the keyboard to mark erroneous lines. The fact that these warning lines slipped through during hectic press runs and appeared in published newspapers turned the phrase "[Etaoin Shrdlu](https://creativepro.com/do-you-know-etaoin-shrdlu/)" into one of the most recognized textual artifacts in printing history.

For those wishing to trace the origins of the Swiss Style from primary sources, Zachary Sauer of Letterform Archive wrote about the archive's [Typografische Monatsblätter](https://letterformarchive.org/news/legacies-of-swiss-style-tyografische-monatsblatter/) (TM) collection. Positioning TM as both a commercial trade publication and a forum where modernist typography was debated, this article is rich in visual material, drawing directly from archival assets with cover designs and page layouts. Within the same historical framework, the book titled "[Lettres Décoratives](https://www.typeroom.eu/the-soul-of-the-french-street-letterform-archive-unveils-lettres-dcoratives)," published by Letterform Archive, compiles specimen and lettering albums used by sign painters in France between 1830 and 1930, bringing visibility to a poorly documented layer of the pre-industrial lettering tradition.

In an [article](https://surfacepodcast.substack.com/p/typography-is-more-than-organizing) written on Nicole Killian's book "[Identity is Variable](https://polymodesans.com/book/)," it is argued that typographic design is not merely a formal arrangement of text, but a process of understanding the identities of the subjects who read and interact with that text. By providing an analytical foundation for how letterforms and typesetting choices function within a sociocultural context, the article questions traditional boundaries within the typography discipline and brings a theoretical framework to this discussion. Comprising 37 essays by 43 authors, "[The Bloomsbury Handbook of Global Typography](https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/bloomsbury-handbook-of-global-typography-9781350336384/)" expands this discussion across geographic and historical breadths. Borna Izadpanah's chapter, tracing the transformation of Nastaliq script into metal type in nineteenth-century Istanbul and Cairo, reevaluates Ottoman and Egyptian print culture through the lens of typographic history.

---

1012.title: The Transformation of Type: From Aesthetics to Engineering
1012.summary: As Volvo prepares for its centenary celebrations in 2027, it treats typography not merely as an aesthetic preference, but directly as a safety parameter. Developed in collaboration with Dalton Maag, the new typeface Volvo Centum bears the character of an engineering project rather than just a brand identity exercise.…
1012.content:
As Volvo prepares for its centenary celebrations in 2027, it treats typography not merely as an aesthetic preference, but directly as a safety parameter. Developed in collaboration with Dalton Maag, the new typeface *[Volvo Centum](https://www.volvocars.com/intl/news/articles/volvo-cars-introduce-typeface-designed-with-safety-in-mind/)* bears the character of an engineering project rather than just a brand identity exercise. Dalton Maag's Creative Director, Zeynep Akay, emphasizes that designing for glance-based reading in motion requires a different mindset, stating that Volvo Centum is designed to maintain its performance under pressure, across different languages, and even at speeds of 100 km/h. This approach represents one of the industrial-scale equivalents of methods based on measuring legibility through objective data, highlighted in Ellen Lupton's article titled "[The Science of Typography](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-bilimi-ellen-lupton-36ebb5196f15)" that we published in 2018. It is remarkable for demonstrating how type design has become an active component of driver safety.

While projects merging design and engineering like the Volvo example come to the fore, innovations on the software side often follow a more cautious and delayed course. The beta version of After Effects will [begin supporting](https://maketypework.com/after-effects-animate-variable-fonts/) variable fonts from the Adobe Fonts library—nearly a decade after their official introduction in 2016. This update, where axes such as weight, width, or slant turn into fluid parameters via keyframes, offers a far more flexible workflow for motion graphic designers.

The diversifying ways typography is utilized also bring legal responsibilities along with them. In [last month's bulletin](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-b%C3%BClteni-aral%C4%B1k-2025-119b6d532a2b), we featured Matthew Butterick's views that because the legal system considers fonts as computer software, copyright strategies must be shaped accordingly. The [guide](https://typeheist.co/blog/font-licensing-for-video-games/) prepared by Laura Eddy for game developers reveals the practical reality of this legal distinction. Eddy states that embedding a font file into a game engine technically and legally falls into the category of *software distribution*, making it a necessity for developers to heed the licensing difference between static images and dynamic code-based text.

While technical and legal boundaries become this clear, the wind is blowing in the exact opposite direction on the commercial side of the industry. The pursuit of perfection is giving way to experimentation. Type foundries are steering toward different strategies, moving away from the traditional *flawless* and *finished product* approach. In his newly published [article](https://revistes.uab.cat/grafica/article/view/ep-ertuk), one of our editors, Murat Ertürk, examines the industry's marketing strategies, the sale of unfinished typefaces, and the rise of experimental sub-brands. Putting pioneering actors such as Future Fonts, Zetafonts, OH no Type Foundry, and Pangram Pangram under the microscope, the study reveals how type foundries deploy their creativity while safeguarding their commercial reputations, and how they involve users in the design process.

---

1013.title: Cultural Memory and the Power of the Archive
1013.summary: While developments on the technological front continue, cultural productions delve into roots, deepening memory. In his review, Ömer Faruk Şerifoğlu examines the book "A Life Dedicated to Fine Arts" by Prof. Dr. İlhami Turan, a doyen of graphic design and typography. As a representative of the Emin Barın tradition,…
1013.content:
While developments on the technological front continue, cultural productions delve into roots, deepening memory. In his [review](https://librekultur.com/kaleme-ve-kagida-adanmis-bir-omur/), Ömer Faruk Şerifoğlu examines the book "A Life Dedicated to Fine Arts" by Prof. Dr. İlhami Turan, a doyen of graphic design and typography. As a representative of the Emin Barın tradition, Turan's 64-year journey extending from Babıali to academia is not just a personal memoir; it serves as a historical document for Turkish typography history, graphic design education, and printing culture. A similar documentation sensitivity emerges across different geographies. Maltese designer Steven Scicluna documents the vanishing tradition of ornament and lettering on Malta's commercial vehicles with his book "[Tberfil: The Art of Maltese Vehicular Decoration in the 20th Century](https://shop.bl.ag/products/tberfil-the-art-of-maltese-vehicular-decoration-in-the-20th-century)". Both examples contribute to the literature by rendering visible, on distinct planes, the manual craftsmanship of the pre-digital era.

Historical references come to life not only in books, but also on ancient stones. In his [article](https://sei.berkeley.edu/2025/12/30/from-stone-to-screen/) exploring a type design process based on Classic Period Maya hieroglyphs and its technical details, Alexandre Bassi details the visual transformation that ancient glyphs—carved in stone with three-dimensional and complex stacking logic—underwent while being adapted to modern digital type technologies and on-screen legibility. Repercussions of US diplomacy's decision to return to Times New Roman continue. In [last month's bulletin](https://medium.com/tipografi/tipografi-b%C3%BClteni-aral%C4%B1k-2025-119b6d532a2b), we reported on the US State Department's decision to return to Times New Roman for official correspondence. Joining this debate, Si Daniels from the Microsoft Design team offers a perspective on what switching between typefaces actually changes, [noting](https://microsoft.design/articles/we-can-all-be-friends-times-new-roman-vs-calibri/) that while both typefaces meet basic conventions in terms of readability, they convey different messages. While Daniels emphasizes that accessibility is no longer ensured solely through typeface selection but can also be achieved through reading modes offered by software, he argues that moving beyond default typefaces is necessary for genuine brand identity. Another bastion of visual memory rises from New York. Reviewed by Creative Review, the [AIGA NY poster archive](https://www.creativereview.co.uk/aiga-ny-poster-archive/) brings together works that bear witness to the last forty years of New York's graphic design scene, created by popular figures such as Stefan Sagmeister and Michael Bierut entirely for their peers, free from commercial concerns. Bearing the marks of the transition from analogue production to the digital era, this visual memory offers an experimental playground where designers pushed the boundaries of typography and composition without client pressure. At the same time, it stands out as a unique collection documenting the city's spirit of cultural and professional solidarity.

---

1008.title: A Shift in the Type Market and Monopolization Debates
1008.summary: In a YouTube video, Harbor Bickmore shares 2025 sales data, pointing to a trend toward professional and direct sales in the type market. While revenues in hobby-oriented marketplaces like Creative Market and Etsy have plummeted dramatically, Monotype revenues and direct sales through the designer's own website are…
1008.content:
In a [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MsPlT9KQEKU) video, Harbor Bickmore shares 2025 sales data, pointing to a trend toward professional and direct sales in the type market. While revenues in hobby-oriented marketplaces like Creative Market and Etsy have plummeted dramatically, Monotype revenues and direct sales through the designer's own website are seeing record increases. As clients avoiding the subscription economy turn toward custom type design commissions, this revenue stream's share of total turnover has reached massive proportions; Bickmore advises designers aiming for a sustainable career to invest in personal type foundry websites supported by Behance and email lists, rather than intermediary platforms. Similarly, a [recent report](https://typenetwork.com/articles/font-sales-figures-type-report) published by Type Network provides concrete data demonstrating that designers focus on aesthetics and quality rather than price when selecting fonts. Of the designers participating in the study, 89.5% stated that they look primarily at overall aesthetics and style before licensing a font, followed by the breadth of the type family. Pricing and licensing terms, however, lag far behind in the decision-making process. Designers turn directly to type foundries' websites 72.4% of the time when searching for fonts, and their motivation to purchase is influenced far more by personal appreciation for the font or admiration for the designer than by discounts. This trend toward independence is also reshaping revenue models across the industry. For instance, in response to declining designer shares, [Font Bros](https://typedrawers.com/discussion/4859/65-now-and-forever-font-bros) is offering a system that proposes a 65% royalty rate for independent type foundries and provides a free website-building infrastructure.

As the commercial structure of the market shifts in this direction, anti-monopoly pushback is also intensifying. We previously addressed the debates fueled by Monotype's acquisition of independent type foundries in our article titled "[Monopolization in the Type Industry](https://medium.com/tipografi/yazı-endüstrisinde-tekelleşme-f100fe18760b)." A new development following up on these debates has emerged. LettError founder Erik van Blokland announced that although his contract with Monotype ended on April 1, 2023, the company continued to sell and license certain typefaces through Monotype, FontShop, and MyFonts channels. Stating that his emails to Monotype on the matter went unanswered, van Blokland launched a website called [Post Mono](https://letterror.com/postmono/) to materialize his protest, embedding a statement directly within the site's code. Furthermore, in a [statement made on LettError's website](https://letterror.com/fonts/fontfonts.html), he declared that the type foundry would never be sold to such an entity. He also emphasized that anyone who purchased any of the typefaces in question through these channels or used them under a subscription after January 1, 2024 does not hold a valid license and must renew their license directly through LettError. In this increasingly complex commercial ecosystem, Doug Wilson, who has a track record of working with global brands, announced [Type Advisor](https://typeadvisor.com/), a typography-focused consulting platform. Developed for creative studios and type foundries, the platform offers expert support in technical areas such as type library strategy, market research, licensing agreement guidance, and accessibility standards. Alongside technical consulting, Wilson aims to bring a holistic consulting approach to the typography industry's complex business processes by providing content-oriented solutions such as copywriting, case studies, and marketing collateral design.

---

1009.title: Typography in the Digital Age: Legibility, Security, and Systems
1009.summary: In digital interfaces, typographic choices go beyond aesthetic considerations to directly affect security and performance. Charles Nix examines how the minimalist construction of ubiquitous typefaces like Arial and Helvetica is weaponized by cyber scammers due to visually indistinguishable letterforms, arguing that…
1009.content:
In digital interfaces, typographic choices go beyond aesthetic considerations to directly affect security and performance. Charles Nix [examines](https://www.fastcompany.com/91489792/how-common-fonts-can-enable-digital-scams) how the minimalist construction of ubiquitous typefaces like Arial and Helvetica is weaponized by cyber scammers due to visually indistinguishable letterforms, arguing that legibility must be prioritized for security. These recommendations are also corroborated by David Březina's [research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13506285.2026.2627306) published in the journal *Visual Cognition*. The study demonstrates that the perception of letter similarity depends not solely on form, but is strongly linked to type design, literacy levels, and contextual evaluations. Jessica Walsh, meanwhile, critiques the typographic monotony of brands, [arguing](https://www.creativeboom.com/insight/typography-might-be-the-last-thing-ai-cant-fake/) that the systematization process prioritizing efficiency erodes unique expression and that typography may be one of the last domains bearing the mark of the human touch in the face of artificial intelligence. On the technical performance side, HTTP Archive's Web Almanac [2025 report](https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2025/fonts#web-font-services) documents that 72% of websites have abandoned external services like Google Fonts in favor of self-hosting their font files, a trend driven by the need to comply with privacy regulations.

Type designers are also re-examining their production tools. In the new version of his personal website, designer Rob Weychert [approaches](https://v7.robweychert.com/blog/2026/01/v7-typographic-scales-and-technical-pens/) typographic scales through a perspective inspired by analog technical drawing tools. Reminding us that before digital production, architects and draftsmen worked with technical pens that provided fixed line weights, Weychert proposes simplifying text hierarchy with a limited number of point sizes and corresponding stroke weights. The article aims to enhance visual consistency and strengthen readability across large, content-heavy pages. Noting that low-contrast typefaces are particularly well suited to this approach, he contends that typographic decisions should be conceived through the logic of tools. Similarly, Harbor Type offers a [guide](https://www.harbortype.com/how-to-animate-variable-fonts-using-python-and-drawbot/) demonstrating how variable fonts can be animated using Drawbot and Python. Finally, in an experimental typeface based on the 13th-century Cistercian numeral system, Bobbie Chen [enables](https://digitalseams.com/blog/making-a-font-with-9999-ligatures-to-display-thirteenth-century-monk-numerals) numbers to automatically transform into medieval symbols by defining 9,999 ligatures via OpenType.

---

1010.title: The Memory of Typography: Archives, Ideologies, and New Visual Identities
1010.summary: The historical and ideological roots of typography are being reintroduced to the literature through new archive projects and corporate identity initiatives. The Typography Debate project, brought to life by Sven Fuchs, gathers digitally the manifestos and polemics that emerged around the New Typography in 20th-century…
1010.content:
The historical and ideological roots of typography are being reintroduced to the literature through new archive projects and corporate identity initiatives. The [Typography Debate](https://typography-debate.org/) project, brought to life by Sven Fuchs, gathers digitally the manifestos and polemics that emerged around the New Typography in 20th-century Europe, reopening modernist typography to re-examination through historical sources as a site of ideological debate. Another contribution to documenting cultural transformation comes from the rare *Meishuzi* manuals added to the [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/this-just-in-chinese-lettering-manuals/). These handbooks document the evolution of modern lettering practices in China's political and commercial communication between 1930 and 1971, as well as the typographic reflections of the simplified character reform. Meanwhile, "[Printing Films](https://printingfilms.com/)," founded by Doug Wilson, presents a rare archive documenting the historical evolution of typography, journalism, and printing technologies. As the heritage of the past is transferred to the web, contemporary state and institutional identities are also being reimagined through custom typographic solutions. The Czech government is renewing the visual identity of state administrations with a custom typeface called [Czechia Sans](https://www.najbrt.cz/en/news/the-visual-identity-of-the-state-administration-of-the-czech-republic), designed by Suitcase Type Foundry. A similar transformation is taking place with the [Hermitage](https://typetype.org/blog/typography-in-the-museum-how-we-developed-the-corporate-typeface-for-the-hermitage/) type family, designed by the TypeType team for the Hermitage Museum. Aiming to reflect historical context without trapping the new typefaces in the aesthetics of a specific era, the project is positioned as the first step in a comprehensive transformation that will reshape the museum's digital identity from the ground up.

---

1019.title: Custom Typeface as an Identity Tool from Jerseys to Official Correspondence
1019.summary: The official typeface of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, FWC26, designed by Pangram Pangram, ensures that the tournament carries a consistent, energetic identity across its brand through a narrow and geometric structure. Oliver Schöndorfer, on the other hand, criticizes FIFA for continuing to use the same typeface for…
1019.content:
The official typeface of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, FWC26, designed by Pangram Pangram, [ensures](https://pimpmytype.com/fifa-2026-font/comment-page-1/#comment-23934) that the tournament carries a consistent, energetic identity across its brand through a narrow and geometric structure. Oliver Schöndorfer, on the other hand, [criticizes](https://pimpmytype.com/fifa-2026-font/) FIFA for continuing to use the same typeface for country abbreviations, even though they replaced FWC26—which suffered from legibility issues—with Noto Sans for the score and timer. This tension between aesthetic identity and functional legibility shows that custom typeface commissions are not always resolved smoothly.

At the club level, similar decisions are shaped by different motivations. Barcelona unveiled [FC Barcelona Modernista](https://www.fcbarcelona.com/en/club/news/4528818/fc-barcelona-presents-new-202627-kit-with-unique-show-at-the-macba-museum?utm_source=chatgpt.com), designed with inspiration from Catalan modernism for their 2026–2027 season kit. Referencing Gaudí's visual language with its vertical proportions and organic lines, the typeface will appear only in Champions League and cup matches, while LaLiga's mandatory typeface will continue to be used in league fixtures. The fruits of the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) lifting its mandatory Arial rule are only just emerging in Turkey. The [custom font](https://www.instagram.com/p/DaXoWQlDD01/) designed by Fatih Hardal for Galatasaray blends the early 2000s outlined lettering heritage with today's minimalist approach, drawing reference from the interlocking structure of the club's 1905 crest and the vertical guide lines of the kit numbers.

The search for institutional identity continues off the pitch as well. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani [adopted](https://www.fastcompany.com/91562875/mayor-mamdani-has-a-new-official-font) Frere-Jones Type's Empirica for official communications. The ongoing collaboration with the campaign designer adds a handcrafted feel inspired by the city's local lettering tradition. It is rare for a candidate to maintain their typographic diligence from the campaign trail after taking office… Ari Zetkin's analysis documenting the 26-year typographic history of the White House website [shows](https://fontsinuse.com/uses/78453/the-typography-of-whitehouse-gov-2000-2026) that this care is the rule rather than the exception. From Bush's three-column interface to Trump's use of Nord Display, every presidential transition has brought its own typeface decision. The selection of a typeface associated with real estate and masculinity can be read through an effort to establish a measured and dignified image of authority.

---

1020.title: Historical Heritage from Artificial Intelligence to Human Hands
1020.summary: A discussion on TypeDrawers revealed the limits of artificial intelligence's relationship with historical material. When John Hudson asked ChatGPT to generate letterforms from late Carolingian manuscripts, the system drew only familiar forms without regard to the source. When a specific manuscript was requested, both…
1020.content:
A [discussion](https://typedrawers.com/discussion/comment/71696/#Comment_71696) on TypeDrawers revealed the limits of artificial intelligence's relationship with historical material. When John Hudson asked ChatGPT to generate letterforms from late Carolingian manuscripts, the system drew only familiar forms without regard to the source. When a specific manuscript was requested, both the dates and the letterforms turned out to be incorrect; moreover, fabricated visuals were presented as if they were authentic source documents. The question Hudson asks is crucial: noting that when a human lies, we understand it alongside sin and the possibility of forgiveness, he asks what our responsibility should be toward an entity incapable of repentance.

Human-led archival practice, by contrast, displays the exact opposite rigor. Letterform Archive's new article series *[Seen Together](https://letterformarchive.org/news/seen-together-chlorodont/)* connects objects in the collection across time. Advertising copy from an Erbar-Grotesk type specimen of the 1930s resurfaces twenty years later in a poster where an art student visualizes a toothache. This unexpected continuity forged by a single consumer product between typography, branding, and design education reminds us of the weight that everyday objects carry in design history.

Obtaining consent and staying faithful to the source are also decisive in revival projects. *Churchward Roundsquare*, used in the posters for Yorgos Lanthimos's film Bugonia, is a typeface discovered by designer Vasilis Marmatakis in the archives of the Te Papa Museum and digitized with permission from Joseph Churchward's daughter. The legacy of Churchward, who refused to use computers and hand-drew 690 typefaces, could only be [brought into the present](https://thespinoff.co.nz/pop-culture/15-11-2025/the-samoan-new-zealand-typographer-behind-the-beloved-bugonia-font) through such a process of permission and research. Slovenian designer Alja Herlah's [Signage Rebirth](https://bl.ag/signage-rebirth-reimagining-slovenias-lettering-heritage/) project shares a similar patience. It reinterprets the original signage lettering of twelve closed or altered Slovenian brands from archival sources, juxtaposing the original design with contemporary interpretations.

Sometimes the value of archival material comes from its imperfections. The vintage digital screens and industrial lettering brought together by Marcin Wichary [show](https://unsung.aresluna.org/good-type-against-all-odds/) that technical limitations can yield an unexpectedly distinctive visual language. In our [March 2026 bulletin](https://open.substack.com/pub/tipografi/p/tipografi-bulteni-mart-2026?r=6ck3m2&selection=8ac5c26e-c192-4dad-bc36-a70a64c56e64&utm_campaign=post-share-selection&utm_medium=web&aspectRatio=instagram&textColor=%23ffffff&bgImage=true), we featured the facade of the Obama Presidential Center, which opened on June 18 in Chicago, as a monumental example of this meticulous approach. Pentagram [inscribed](https://www.printmag.com/architecture/typography-has-its-monumental-moment-at-the-obama-presidential-center/) 103 words selected from a speech Obama delivered in 2015 into the building's facade using 1.3-meter-tall Gotham letters. Up close, the physical presence of the letters stands out, while from a distance, the entire composition integrates with the city's skyline.

---

1021.title: Different Design and Marketing Pursuits in New Type Families
1021.summary: The common thread among new type families this month is that the rationale behind design decisions is made visible as well. Designed for Strasbourg's UNESCO World Book Capital project and released for free, Azimut transforms the classical weight structure into three independent yet harmonious styles. In this system…
1021.content:
The common thread among new type families this month is that the rationale behind design decisions is made visible as well. Designed for Strasbourg's UNESCO World Book Capital project and released for free, Azimut transforms the classical weight structure into three independent yet harmonious styles. In this system [reviewed by Dan Reynolds](https://azimut.strasbourg.eu/english.html#DR), uppercase letters are designed with the same width across all three styles; users can create decorative arrangements by switching between styles without needing knowledge of OpenType or kerning. Referencing Gerrit Noordzij's definition of typography as writing with prefabricated letters, Reynolds suggests that Azimut embodies this concept for today's reader.

Sometimes the source of inspiration is not a corporate commission, but the very surfaces of the city. [Olivier Gourvat](https://oliviergourvat.com/) [designed](https://www.printmag.com/type-tuesday/type-tuesday-calenza-proves-the-best-type-museums-are-city-streets/?mc_cid=4343328ef6&mc_eid=48a95a3cf1#utm_source=The+League+of+Moveable+Type) [Calenza](https://www.motyfo.com/calenza/) by studying Valencia's ceramic street plaques in use since 1902. The narrow letterforms produced by sign painters by squeezing long street names form the starting point for the type family's three members: normal, condensed, and compressed. Quirky letterforms rarely encountered in the city were also included in the family.

We value the processes behind typeface designs and make a point of featuring them in our bulletins. Announced by Mass-Driver after a five-year development process, [MD UI](https://mass-driver.com/typefaces/md-ui/) [presents](https://mass-driver.com/article/md-ui-a-typeface-for-interfacing) a striking example of this approach by bringing together 48 static styles across three optical sizes into a single variable font. It is also noteworthy that the type foundry chose to refresh its own visual identity with the new typeface rather than announcing it through a separate promotional campaign. A similar meticulousness is [evident](https://elementtype.co/opet-italic/) in Element Type's collaboration with Opet. Taking the 2004 logo as a starting point, the type foundry redesigned the letters from scratch and expanded the typeface's character set to support over a hundred languages.

Beyond the design process, how type is sold is also a topic of this month's bulletin. Having published typefaces designed for brands on Google Fonts for a long time, Koto established its own type foundry, [CCType](https://cctype.com/), and [made its debut](https://www.itsnicethat.com/articles/koto-cctype-typography-project-080726) with [CC Timeline](https://cctype.com/typefaces/cc-timeline). Combining British movable type with Swiss-German modernist phototypesetting influences, the family adopts a one-time purchase model instead of traditional licensing. In his [article](https://revistes.uab.cat/grafica/article/view/ep-ertuk) examining the marketing strategies of type foundries, one of our editors, [Murat Ertürk](https://www.muraterturk.com/), had pointed out the industry's tendency to move away from conventional sales models.

1022.title: Small Points
1022.summary: 📁 Bursa's local lettering archive YaziBursa.com has launched. 🆕 Ahmet Altun released Maride, a new typeface consisting of ten weights. 🔎 Fontastic Space compares typefaces in the Google Fonts library by anatomical features and OpenType metrics, generating ready-to-use CSS code. 🗺️ Arcotype maps typefaces by visual…
1022.content:
📁 Bursa's local lettering archive [YaziBursa.com](https://www.yazibursa.com/) has launched.

🆕 Ahmet Altun released [Maride](https://www.fontspring.com/fonts/ahmet-altun/maride), a new typeface consisting of ten weights.

🔎 [Fontastic Space](https://fontastic.space/) compares typefaces in the Google Fonts library by anatomical features and OpenType metrics, generating ready-to-use CSS code.

🗺️ [Arcotype](https://www.arcoty.pe/) maps typefaces by visual similarity, promising to steer away from overused choices.

🔡 [Yep! Type](https://yeptype.com/) [examines](https://yeptype.com/article/when-to-use-retalic-fonts) left-leaning typefaces that can be used to create emphasis and a sense of motion, accompanied by examples.

🎓 The "[Armenian Printers of Istanbul](https://www.instagram.com/p/DaXnGAWIpR8/)" workshop will be held in Yerevan on August 7–8, 2026.

🏛️ With a new bill, the Parliament of Uzbekistan has [come closer](https://www.bbc.com/turkce/articles/cyv0ll4j081o) to completing its 33-year transition to the Latin alphabet.

📚 The revised second edition of the book "[How to Create Typefaces](https://shop.itemzero.com/products/how-to-create-typefaces/)" has been published.
